items.q: Why are wired connections still preferred in many industrial IoT settings despite wireless dominating consumer IoT?
options: They offer high throughput, deterministic timing, and reliability/security critical for mission-critical systems
items.explain: Wired links provide determinism, reliability, and security that industrial control needs. Wireless wins on flexibility/cost but can't guarantee timing the way deterministic Ethernet can.

items.q: A 'constrained-node network' in IoT refers to:
options: A network of devices with limited CPU, memory, and battery, plus low bandwidth and high loss
A network limited to exactly 10 nodes
items.explain: Constrained devices have tight CPU/memory/power limits; constrained-node networks of them have low bandwidth, high loss, and strict power budgets — hence lightweight protocols like CoAP.

items.q: Ethernet is standardized as ___ and defines which OSI layers?
items.explain: Ethernet = IEEE 802.3, defining the physical and data-link layers. (802.11 is Wi-Fi; 802.15.4 underlies Zigbee; 802.1 includes TSN.)

items.q: In an Ethernet IoT LAN, which device operates at Layer 2 using MAC addresses to forward frames only to the intended recipient?
items.explain: The switch forwards frames at Layer 2 using MAC addresses (no broadcast flooding). The router operates at Layer 3, performing NAT and routing to the WAN/internet.

items.q: Which correctly distinguishes a MAC address from an IP address?
options: MAC is logical and routable; IP is a hardware ID
MAC is a hardware ID for local (Layer-2) delivery; IP is a logical address for routing across networks (Layer 3)
MAC is only used on the internet; IP only on LANs
items.explain: MAC = unique hardware identifier for delivery within the local network (Layer 2). IP = logical identifier for routing packets across networks/the internet (Layer 3).

items.q: What is the primary benefit of Power over Ethernet (PoE)?
options: It doubles the data rate of Ethernet
A single cable carries both data and electrical power, removing the need for separate power wiring
It works only with fibre optics
It eliminates the need for any network connection
items.explain: PoE delivers data + power on one Ethernet cable, so devices like cameras and sensors can be placed where there's no power outlet — one cable, one install.

items.q: Order the PoE standards by increasing power: 802.3af, 802.3at, 802.3bt.
items.explain: 802.3af ≈15.4 W → 802.3at (PoE+) ≈30 W → 802.3bt (PoE++) ≈60/90 W. In the device labels: PSE sources power, PD receives it.

items.q: Why is plain Ethernet insufficient for cyber-physical systems, motivating TSN?
options: Plain Ethernet is best-effort — it cannot guarantee WHEN a packet arrives (no bounded latency/jitter)
items.explain: Standard Ethernet is best-effort, fine for email/video but not for systems needing guaranteed timing. TSN (IEEE 802.1) adds determinism: bounded latency and minimal jitter.

items.q: Which TSN feature synchronizes all devices' clocks to sub-microsecond precision?
items.explain: 802.1AS provides precise time synchronization, enabling coordinated action between sensors and actuators. Qbv schedules traffic, Qbu preempts frames, Qcc reserves bandwidth.

items.q: Power Line Communication (PLC) transmits data by:
options: Overlaying high-frequency data signals (kHz–MHz) on existing AC power lines, separated from the 50/60 Hz power by filters
items.explain: PLC reuses existing electrical wiring: data (kHz–MHz, via OFDM/FSK/PSK) rides on top of the 50/60 Hz power, with filters separating the two. Popular in smart grids/meters.

items.q: Why do most consumer IoT technologies use unlicensed frequency bands?
options: They offer the highest possible data rates
Cost-free access, globally harmonized standards, and scalability — IoT devices can't afford licensed spectrum
They are reserved exclusively for one vendor
items.explain: Unlicensed bands (e.g., 2.4 GHz ISM) need no licence fee, are globally harmonized, and let billions of cheap devices coexist — though the trade-off is interference in a crowded commons.

items.q: Which technology does NOT use unlicensed spectrum?
items.explain: NB-IoT (and LTE-M, 4G/5G) are cellular and use LICENSED spectrum managed by operators. Zigbee, Wi-Fi, and LoRa all use unlicensed bands.

items.q: By range, NFC/RFID, Wi-Fi, and LoRa belong respectively to which classes?
options: Short (<10 cm), medium (~100 m–km), long (LPWAN, tens of km)
items.explain: NFC/RFID is short-range (<10 cm); Wi-Fi is medium-range; LoRa is long-range LPWAN (tens of km). Range trades off against data rate and power.

items.q: Zigbee is built on which standard and operates mainly in which band?
items.explain: Zigbee is built on IEEE 802.15.4 and operates mainly in the 2.4 GHz unlicensed ISM band (with sub-GHz regional variants), using AES-128 and mesh networking.

items.q: In a Zigbee network, which device starts the PAN, picks the channel/PAN ID, and often acts as the Trust Center?
items.explain: The Coordinator (one per network) starts the PAN, selects the channel and PAN ID, holds network keys, and often serves as Trust Center and hub. Routers relay; end devices sleep and don't relay.

items.q: How does a battery-powered Zigbee End Device conserve power yet still receive data?
options: It sleeps; its router 'parent' buffers downlink frames, and the end device sends a MAC Data Request to pull them when it wakes
It uses a permanent mains connection
items.explain: End devices sleep to save power and cannot relay. A parent router buffers their messages; on waking, the end device requests the queued data — enabling years of coin-cell life.

items.q: Approximately how much less power does BLE consume compared to Classic Bluetooth, and why?
options: About the same; both stay always on
~100× less, because BLE stays in sleep mode except during brief connections
BLE uses no power at all
items.explain: BLE consumes roughly 100× less power than Classic Bluetooth because it sleeps most of the time, waking only to send/receive small packets — unlike always-on Classic Bluetooth.

items.q: In BLE, the application data model that defines services and characteristics is:
items.explain: GATT defines the data model — services (e.g., Heart Rate) and characteristics (values). GAP handles discovery, advertising, connections, and roles (central/peripheral).

items.q: In the BLE lifecycle, a peripheral first announces its existence by:
options: Advertising — sending short packets on channels 37/38/39 with its name and service UUIDs
items.explain: The peripheral advertises on channels 37/38/39 ('I exist' + basic info). A central then scans, connects, pairs/bonds, discovers GATT services, and streams data.

items.q: Wi-Fi's biggest advantage for IoT compared to Zigbee/BLE is:
options: It uses the least power of all
Native IP connectivity over existing infrastructure — no gateway translation needed to reach the cloud
It supports the most devices on a coin cell
items.explain: Wi-Fi devices are natively IP and join existing networks, reaching the cloud without a translating gateway (unlike Zigbee/BLE). Its drawback is high power — hence Wi-Fi HaLow for low-power IoT.

items.q: Wi-Fi HaLow (802.11ah) differs from standard Wi-Fi by:
options: Operating in sub-GHz (~900 MHz) for longer range and lower power, tuned for IoT
items.explain: Wi-Fi HaLow uses sub-GHz (~900 MHz) to trade raw speed for much longer range and lower power — letting battery IoT devices use Wi-Fi-family networking.

items.q: LoRaWAN uses which network topology?
items.explain: LoRaWAN uses a star-of-stars: end devices broadcast to all nearby gateways (a star), and gateways relay to one central network server (another star). Gateways are transparent relays.

items.q: Which LoRaWAN device class offers the BEST battery life by only opening receive windows after an uplink?
items.explain: Class A (the default for most sensors) opens two short receive windows only after sending an uplink — maximizing battery life. Class C keeps the receiver always open (mains-powered); Class B uses scheduled slots.

items.q: In LoRaWAN security, which key ensures data CONFIDENTIALITY between the device and application server?
items.explain: The AppSKey ensures confidentiality (prevents eavesdropping) between device and application server. The NwkSKey ensures integrity (anti-tampering) between device and network server.

items.q: In the LoRaWAN architecture, which component performs de-duplication, device authentication, and Adaptive Data Rate?
items.explain: The Network Server is the 'brain' — it de-duplicates packets from multiple gateways, authenticates devices, runs ADR, routes data, and manages security. Gateways are transparent relays.

items.q: How does cellular IoT (NB-IoT, LTE-M) fundamentally differ from Zigbee/LoRa?
options: It uses LICENSED spectrum operated by telecom carriers (no self-deployed gateways needed)
items.explain: Cellular IoT runs on licensed, carrier-managed spectrum — giving ubiquitous coverage with no gateway deployment, at the cost of a recurring subscription. Zigbee/LoRa use unlicensed bands.

items.q: Which best contrasts NB-IoT and LTE-M?
options: NB-IoT supports high mobility and voice; LTE-M is stationary only
NB-IoT = lowest power, deep coverage, stationary low-rate; LTE-M = higher rate, supports mobility and voice
items.explain: NB-IoT targets ultra-low-power, deep-indoor, stationary sensors at very low data rates. LTE-M offers more bandwidth plus mobility (handover) and voice — for moving/richer devices.

items.q: Which pair correctly matches the IoT application-layer communication models to protocols?
options: Publish/Subscribe: HTTP, CoAP; Request/Response: MQTT, AMQP
Publish/Subscribe: MQTT, AMQP; Request/Response: HTTP, CoAP
items.explain: Message-oriented publish/subscribe (broker, decoupled): MQTT, AMQP. Request/response (client-server): HTTP, CoAP.

items.q: The key advantage of the publish/subscribe model for scalable IoT is that:
options: Publishers and subscribers must always be online together
Publishers and subscribers are decoupled via a broker/topics — neither needs to know the other, enabling intermittent, scalable communication
It only works for two devices
items.explain: Pub/sub decouples senders from receivers through a broker and topics (like a noticeboard), so thousands of intermittently-connected devices can communicate without direct, simultaneous connections.

items.q: In MQTT, what is the role of the broker?
options: It is the central server that routes messages from publishers to all clients subscribed to the matching topic
It encrypts data using DTLS only
It replaces the need for any clients
items.explain: The MQTT broker receives messages tagged with a topic from publishers and delivers them to all subscribers of that topic — decoupling the two sides.

items.q: Which MQTT QoS level guarantees a message is delivered EXACTLY once?
items.explain: QoS 2 uses a handshake to deliver exactly once (for financial/control data). QoS 0 is fire-and-forget; QoS 1 guarantees arrival but may duplicate.

items.q: MQTT's 'Last Will and Testament' (LWT) feature is used to:
options: Notify other clients with a predefined message if a client disconnects unexpectedly
items.explain: LWT lets the broker publish a predefined 'last will' message when a client drops unexpectedly, so other clients learn of the failure. (Retained messages serve new subscribers the last value.)

items.q: CoAP is often described as 'HTTP for tiny things' because it:
options: Runs over TCP with large headers
Uses a RESTful model (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) but runs primarily over UDP with tiny headers and no TCP handshake
items.explain: CoAP keeps HTTP's RESTful resource model and methods but runs over UDP with compact binary headers and built-in reliability — efficient for constrained devices. It also supports multicast and discovery.

items.q: Which row of the CoAP vs HTTP vs MQTT comparison is CORRECT?
options: CoAP: TCP, MQTT: UDP, HTTP: UDP
CoAP: UDP + DTLS + request/response (with Observe); MQTT: TCP + pub/sub; HTTP: TCP + request/response
items.explain: CoAP = UDP, DTLS security, request/response + Observe, supports multicast. MQTT = TCP, TLS, publish/subscribe. HTTP = TCP, TLS, request/response, web-focused.

items.q: SCADA systems are best described as:
options: Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition — architectures for monitoring/controlling industrial processes (field devices, RTUs/PLCs, network, master/HMI)
items.explain: SCADA = Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition: field sensors/actuators, RTUs/PLCs, a communication network (Modbus/DNP3/IP), and a central master with an HMI for operators — 'industrial IoT before IoT'.

items.q: A common IoT integration pattern uses lightweight protocols at the edge and converts to ___ at the gateway/cloud for web integration.
items.explain: Edge devices run CoAP/MQTT (lightweight), and the gateway/cloud converts to HTTP/REST — which every web service, browser, and app already speaks — for easy integration.
